claims.question: q2
claims.claim: Microsoft’s GraphRAG system improved answer comprehensiveness by 26% and diversity by 57% versus standard vector retrieval in Microsoft’s own benchmarks.
claims.quote: Microsoft’s GraphRAG system improved answer comprehensiveness by 26% and diversity by 57% compared to standard vector retrieval in their own benchmarks.

claims.question: q2
claims.claim: GraphRAG indexing is far more expensive than vector embedding: the same corpus costs under $5 to embed in a vector database but $50-200 through GraphRAG’s entity extraction and community summarization pipeline.
claims.quote: Then you look at the indexing bill: the same corpus that costs under $5 to embed into a vector database runs $50-200 through GraphRAG’s entity extraction and community summarization pipeline.

claims.question: q2
claims.claim: LightRAG indexes a 500-page corpus in about 3 minutes for roughly $0.50 and achieves 70-90% of GraphRAG’s performance at 1/100th the cost.
claims.quote: Indexing the same 500-page corpus takes about 3 minutes and costs roughly $0.50. Quality benchmarks show 70-90% of GraphRAG’s performance at 1/100th the cost.

claims.question: q2
claims.claim: Vector RAG is sufficient for direct factual lookups that map to single chunks; adding a knowledge graph to such use cases adds cost and complexity without improving accuracy.
claims.quote: Vector RAG handles direct factual lookups efficiently: “What is our return policy?” “When does the contract expire?” These queries map cleanly to single chunks. Adding a knowledge graph to this use case adds cost and complexity without improving accuracy.

claims.question: q1
claims.claim: Graph RAG adds a knowledge graph layer between documents and retrieval, traversing relationships between entities such as people, companies, concepts, and events instead of relying only on similar text search.
claims.quote: Graph RAG adds a knowledge graph layer between your documents and the retrieval step. Instead of searching for similar text, the system traverses relationships between entities: people, companies, concepts, events.

claims.question: q5
claims.claim: Microsoft GraphRAG uses LLM-powered open-ended extraction in which the model decides what entities and relationships exist; this is useful for exploration but produces noisy graphs at scale.
claims.quote: Microsoft GraphRAG sidesteps this by using LLM-powered open-ended extraction: the model decides what entities and relationships exist. This works for exploration but produces noisy graphs at scale.

claims.question: q5
claims.claim: The article states that the hardest part of Graph RAG is designing the ontology—which entity types matter, which relationship types to extract, and how granular to go.
claims.quote: The hardest part of Graph RAG is not the framework. It is designing the ontology: which entity types matter, what relationship types to extract, how granular to go.
